text: Some observations from a retiree: If you are relatively young, a good approach would be to invest in capital appreciation/growth over dividend growth. In this scenario, ten year historical returns, statistics show that VOO has outpaced SCHD for capital appreciation/growth. For dividend growth, SCHD has outpaced VOO. People seem to disregard VOO because they do not realize VOO does have dividend growth, although that dividend growth is not as steady as SCHD. The most important stat for long term investors, though, is total return. Total return is the result of capital appreciation plus dividends. Over that ten year time frame, VOO has beaten SCHD in total return.  People get so intrigued with the higher dividend yield of SCHD that they ignore the fact that total return, especially when building a portfolio when you are young is really MORE important. I can understand that as a person gets older, that they may prefer the higher dividend income of SCHD. However, if the goal is to build wealth for retirement, using ETFs that have a higher total return is more beneficial. Nothing against SCHD, though, because it is a bit more "steady", but at the end of the day, it is better to have more total capital (wealth). You can always transition to SCHD later in life because it will probably be less volatile. That stated, be sure not to panic during market downturns. I invested in the S&P 500 during my career. When the stock market crashed during 2000 and 2008 periods, I continued investing. Some of my co-workers reacted, and pulled their money from the market (especially in their 401Ks) during the crashes and never got back in soon enough. It is really hard to "time the market". I wasn't going to be retiring anytime soon (during those time periods), so I continued buying the S&P 500 at it lower, "bargain" prices. When the market came back up, my portfolio really shined. Of course, that stated, past performance is no guarantee of future returns. This worked for me, but nobody really knows what will happen in the future. Good luck (and keep investing).
